questions.q: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023, which replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973, came into force with effect from:
questions.src: BNSS 2023 — notified effective 1 July 2024, confirmed across multiple 2025-2026 legal sources; syllabus (ucl.osmania.ac.in) mandates comparative study of BNSS with old CrPC

questions.q: Under BNSS, provisions relating to arrest of persons (with or without warrant, rights of arrested persons) are covered under which Sections?
questions.src: Osmania University V Semester syllabus (official PDF) — 'Arrest of Persons (Sec. 35 to 62)' explicitly listed under BNSS

questions.q: Under BNSS, a person arrested without a warrant must be produced before the nearest Magistrate within:
o: 24 hours, excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's court
questions.src: BNSS — continuation of the constitutional safeguard under Article 22(2); 24-hour production requirement (excluding journey time) carried forward from CrPC Section 57 into BNSS

questions.q: Under BNSS, when a person is arrested, they have the right to:
o: Remain silent about their identity only
Be informed of the grounds of arrest and, if arrested without warrant, the right to have a friend/relative/person of choice informed of the arrest and place of detention
No specific rights until formally charged
Only consult a lawyer after 7 days
questions.src: BNSS — carries forward the D.K. Basu safeguards and constitutional right to be informed of grounds of arrest, plus the right to have someone informed of the arrest

questions.q: Under BNSS, provisions relating to 'Information to Police' and FIR (First Information Report) are covered under which Sections?
questions.src: Osmania University V Semester syllabus — 'Information to Police-FIR (Section 173 To 196)' explicitly listed under BNSS

questions.q: Under BNSS, for offences punishable with imprisonment of 3 years or more but less than 7 years, before registering an FIR, a police officer may (with permission of a senior officer) conduct a preliminary enquiry to ascertain if a prima facie case exists, within:
questions.src: BNSS Section 173 — introduces a new preliminary enquiry mechanism (within 14 days per most authoritative summaries; some sources cite this differently, so verify with your faculty) for offences in the 3-7 year punishment range before mandatory FIR registration

questions.q: Under BNSS, provisions dealing with 'Preventive Action of the Police', unlawful assembly, and public nuisance are covered under which Sections?
questions.src: Osmania University V Semester syllabus — 'Maintenance of Public Order and Tranquillity-Unlawful Assembly- Public Nuisance...Preventive Action of the Police (Sec. 148 To 172)' explicitly listed

questions.q: Under BNSS, provisions relating to maintenance of wife, children, and parents are covered under which Sections?
questions.src: Osmania University V Semester syllabus — 'Maintenance of Wife, Children and Parents (Sec. 144 To 147)' explicitly listed under BNSS

questions.q: The maintenance provision under BNSS (previously Section 125 CrPC) allows a Magistrate to order maintenance for a wife, children, or parents who are unable to maintain themselves. This remedy is available:
o: Irrespective of the religion of the parties — it is a secular, religion-neutral provision
Only if there is no other civil remedy available
Only for children, not wives or parents
questions.src: Settled principle carried forward into BNSS — the maintenance provision is secular and applies irrespective of religion (as under the corresponding CrPC Section 125 jurisprudence)

questions.q: Under BNSS, provisions relating to 'Security for Keeping Peace and Good Behaviour' are covered under which Sections?
questions.src: Osmania University V Semester syllabus — 'Security for Keeping Peace and Good Behaviour (Sec. 125 To 143)' explicitly listed under BNSS

questions.q: Under BNSS, provisions dealing with 'Proclamation and Attachment of Property' (in respect of a person absconding to avoid arrest) are covered under which Sections?
questions.src: Osmania University V Semester syllabus — 'Proclamation and Attachment of Property (Section 63 To 93)' explicitly listed under BNSS

questions.q: Under BNSS, provisions relating to Plea Bargaining are covered under which Sections?
questions.src: Osmania University V Semester syllabus — 'Plea Bargaining (Sec. 289 To 300)' explicitly listed under BNSS

questions.q: Plea bargaining under BNSS is generally available for offences where the maximum punishment prescribed is:
o: Any offence, including those punishable with death or life imprisonment
Imprisonment up to 7 years (excluding offences affecting the socio-economic condition of the country, and offences against women and children below 14 years)
Only offences under special local laws
questions.src: Settled principle carried forward into BNSS from CrPC — plea bargaining excluded for offences punishable with death/life imprisonment/more than 7 years, and specific excluded categories (women/child victims below 14, socio-economic offences)

questions.q: Under BNSS, general provisions relating to Bails and Bonds are covered under which Sections?
questions.src: Osmania University V Semester syllabus — 'Provisions as to Bails And Bonds (Sec. 478 to 496)' explicitly listed under BNSS

questions.q: Under BNSS, an important change regarding undertrial prisoners is that a first-time offender who has undergone detention for a period extending up to what fraction of the maximum sentence prescribed may be released on bond (subject to conditions)?
questions.src: BNSS introduces a new provision benefiting first-time offenders — release on bond after undergoing detention for one-half of the maximum sentence, a change from the CrPC undertrial-release framework

questions.q: Under BNSS, 'General Provisions as to Inquiries and Trial' are covered under which Sections?
questions.src: Osmania University V Semester syllabus — 'General Provisions as Inquiries & Trial (Sec.337-378)' explicitly listed under BNSS

questions.q: A notable feature introduced/strengthened under BNSS, allowing an FIR to be registered at any police station irrespective of where the offence occurred (to be later transferred to the appropriate jurisdiction), is known as:
questions.src: Zero FIR concept — formally recognised and strengthened under BNSS, allowing registration at any police station regardless of jurisdiction, with mandatory transfer to the appropriate station

questions.q: A significant procedural change under BNSS, as compared to the earlier CrPC, is the mandatory/encouraged use of:
o: Handwritten records only, with no digital provisions
Audio-video electronic means for recording of search and seizure procedures, and provisions enabling electronic filing/service of summons in certain circumstances
Only postal summons, with no electronic mode permitted
No change from CrPC on this aspect
questions.src: BNSS emphasizes technology integration — audio-video recording of search/seizure, provisions for electronic communication/service — a notable shift from the CrPC 1973 framework

questions.q: Under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015, a 'child in conflict with law' refers to a child who is alleged or found to have committed an offence and who, on the date of commission of the offence, had not completed:
questions.src: Juvenile Justice Act 2015, Section 2(13) — 'child in conflict with law' defined as a person below 18 years alleged/found to have committed an offence

questions.q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act 2015, a child aged 16-18 years alleged to have committed a 'heinous offence' (punishable with 7+ years imprisonment) may, after preliminary assessment by the Juvenile Justice Board, be:
o: Automatically tried as an adult without any assessment
Tried as an adult in a Children's Court, if the Board finds the child has the mental and physical capacity to commit the offence and understand its consequences
Never tried as an adult under any circumstances
questions.src: Juvenile Justice Act 2015, Sections 15-19 — the preliminary assessment mechanism for 16-18 year-olds in heinous offence cases, allowing potential trial as an adult after Board assessment; a significant post-Nirbhaya-case reform

questions.q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act 2015, the body responsible for inquiring into cases of children in conflict with law is the:
questions.src: Juvenile Justice Act 2015 — the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) handles children in conflict with law, while the Child Welfare Committee (CWC) handles children in need of care and protection

questions.q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act 2015, the body responsible for children in need of care and protection (as distinct from children in conflict with law) is the:
o: National Commission for Protection of Child Rights
questions.src: Juvenile Justice Act 2015 — Child Welfare Committee (CWC) handles children in need of care and protection; distinct from the JJB which handles children in conflict with law

questions.q: Under the Probation of Offenders Act 1958, the underlying philosophy of releasing a first-time or minor offender on probation instead of imprisonment reflects which theory of punishment?
questions.src: Probation of Offenders Act 1958 — settled principle that probation reflects the reformative (rehabilitative) theory of punishment, focusing on reforming the offender rather than punishing

questions.q: Under the Probation of Offenders Act 1958, a court may release an offender on probation of good conduct instead of sentencing them to imprisonment, generally for offences NOT punishable with:
questions.src: Probation of Offenders Act 1958 — probation is generally not available for offences punishable with death or imprisonment for life, reserved for less serious offences

questions.q: Which of the following is recognised as a modern 'correctional method' in criminal justice administration, alongside imprisonment, aimed at reformation rather than pure punishment?
o: Probation, parole, and open prisons/correctional institutions aimed at reintegration into society
questions.src: Settled criminology/correctional-methods principle — probation, parole, and open/correctional institutions represent modern reformative approaches, distinct from purely punitive methods

questions.q: The Supreme Court in Lalita Kumari v. State of UP (2014) held that a preliminary enquiry before FIR registration could only ascertain whether the information discloses a cognizable offence. How does Section 173(3) BNSS 2023 depart from this position for offences punishable with 3-7 years imprisonment?
o: It abolishes preliminary enquiry entirely, requiring immediate FIR registration in all cases

It broadens the permissible scope of preliminary enquiry beyond merely checking if a cognizable offence is disclosed — to assessing whether a 'prima facie case' exists for proceeding, a wider threshold than Lalita Kumari originally permitted for this specific offence band
It applies Lalita Kumari's exact test with zero modification
It removes police discretion entirely and hands the decision to the Magistrate alone
questions.src: Section 173(3) BNSS 2023, as analysed by the Supreme Court in Imran Pratapgadhi v. State of Gujarat (2025) — for the 3-7 year offence band, BNSS permits a broader 'prima facie case' enquiry, a genuine departure from Lalita Kumari's narrower 'discloses a cognizable offence' test; this remains an actively debated/evolving area of BNSS jurisprudence, so exact contours may continue to develop through further judicial interpretation

questions.q: A wife files for maintenance under the BNSS's maintenance provisions (the successor to CrPC Section 125). The husband argues the claim must fail because a civil maintenance suit is also pending between the parties. What is the settled position on this argument?
o: The BNSS maintenance remedy is automatically barred whenever ANY other civil remedy exists or is pending

The BNSS/erstwhile Section 125 maintenance remedy is a summary, independent statutory remedy that generally survives ALONGSIDE any civil remedy — the existence of a separate civil suit does not by itself bar the summary maintenance application, though courts may account for amounts already awarded to avoid double recovery
The wife must always choose one remedy and permanently waive the other
Maintenance claims are only valid if no civil suit was ever filed
questions.src: Settled principle carried forward — maintenance under this provision is a summary, independent remedy that generally coexists with civil remedies (though courts adjust for double-counting of amounts), a frequently tested point since students often assume civil pendency automatically bars the summary claim

questions.q: A 17-year-old is alleged to have committed a heinous offence. The Juvenile Justice Board conducts a preliminary assessment under the JJ Act 2015 and forms the opinion that the child has the mental/physical capacity to commit the offence and understand its consequences. What is the LEGAL EFFECT of this specific finding?
o: The child is automatically sentenced to the adult maximum punishment with no further process

The case may be transferred for trial as an adult before the Children's Court, but the child is still NOT automatically subjected to the same punishment regime as an adult in every respect — the JJ Act's protective framework (e.g., prohibition on death penalty/life imprisonment without possibility of release for the juvenile, placement in a place of safety rather than adult prison in specified circumstances) continues to apply even after such transfer
The child is released immediately with no further proceedings
The Board's preliminary assessment finding is final and cannot be reviewed by the Children's Court at all
questions.src: Juvenile Justice Act 2015, Sections 15-19 — even where a case is transferred to the Children's Court after preliminary assessment, the Act's protective safeguards (e.g., no death penalty/life imprisonment without release possibility for the juvenile, requirements around place of safety) continue to apply — a nuance students often miss, assuming transfer means full adult treatment in every respect
